He said :	In respectfully asking the
House permission to refer this Bill back to the Railway Committee, I hope I will be allowed to give a few words of explanation. tee, but I have heard that strong objection had been taken to the Bill on account of the further and extensive powers asked by the company, and that if the promoters had been satisfied with asking an extension of time to enable them to go on with their work and carry out the powers already granted them by parliament there would have been no objection. G787 COMMONS BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to know from the government when we shall have all government legislation and all government estimates before the House ? I brought the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister three of four weeks ago, and I was fihen informed that a statement would be made. I believe that statement was made some time afterwards, but I am not quite sure it has been actually adhered to, and possibly there are other government measures which were not contemplated at that time, although I do not think any should be brought down which were not then announced. However, no doubt the Prime Minister is able to make a complete and accurate statement to us now. It is certainly time that all government measures were brought before the House ; it is certainly time all railway subsidies, if any, were brought before the House ; and it is certainly time that government estimates, whether for the ensuing year or the present year, were before the House-that is, if we propose to finish the session at any reasonable date. It is for that reason that I now bring the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: G787 COMMONS BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: When my hon. friend called my attention to this matter some time ago, I stated that it was not the intention of the government to bring any more legislation this session, except perhaps a few matters of purely departmental character. I may say to my hon. friend that it is not contemplated by the government to introduce any more legislation of any kind whatever, except what is to-day on the order paper, with this exception: that as I have already stated, it is the intention of the government to bring some legislation with regai d to the acquisition of the Canada Eastern Railway. That has not yet been given notice of, but everything else contemplated by the government has been given notice of. The Bills which are contemplated to be introduced have all been given notice of and stand on the order paper for first reading, which I expect will be given them either on Monday or Tuesday. With regard to railway subsidies, as at present advised and I think I can safely say, it is not the intention of the government to bring any railway subsidies this year ; perhaps some legislation may be introduced with regard to existing subsidies, but no new subsidies at all. With regard to the estimates, my hon friend is quite right in saying that it is time we should have them, and I hope to have them probably on Tuesday next without committing myself absolutely ; certainly Tuesday or the day after.

maintopic: G787 COMMONS BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The order paper instead of growing smaller appears to be growing larger. There are five Bills to be introduced Mr. WRIGHT.
by the government and five resolutions, which mean five Bills more to be founded upon them. One of the most important Bills of the whole session will be, I have no doubt, the Canada Eastern Railway Bill. In my judgment a Bill of that importance should net be brought into the House at the tail end of the session, because it makes it utterly impossible for members of parliament to institute such inquiry as they ought to, in order to enable them to deal with it intelligently. They have not time to do it because it is rushed through in a few days. This is too important a measure to be allowed to pass this House in this way, and I respectfully submit fihat if it is the intention of the government to deal with that question it should have been brought down at an earlier date. It is an injustice to the House and to the country as well, that we are called upon to deal with a Bill of that importance, at a time it is utterly impossible to do so with the care that we ought to exercise in the interests of all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend the Prime Minister informs me that he omitted to mention a possible amendment to the Banking Act. Might I call the attention of the right hon. the Prime Minister to the delay in the work at the Printing Bureau. The lists for my county were brought down in the month of December. and I was promised by the King's Printer that I would receive them at the end of January. We are now nearly at the end of July and I have not heard of them yet. Some time ago I called at the Bureau to inquire and saw Mr. Smith who has charge of the printing. Mr. Smith seems to be an efficient officer but he explained to me that it was impossible during the session to look after the lists with the facilities at their disposal. If we are to have six or eight month sessions and if during that time the printing of the lists will be delayed, a great deal of inconvenience will be caused, and it seems to me that if the government cannot have the work done at the Printing Bureau they should see that the lists are printed outside.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It has, I think, been found that it is preferable that the lists should be printed at the Printing
Bureau. I am sorry to say that the capacity of the Bureau is not adequate to the requirements of the business. I think that the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has the intention to ask parliament for an appropriation for extending the space available at the Bureau, and with the increased space it may be possible to give satisfaction to my hon. friend who is not by any means the only complainant.
Wait until the new building is up and you will get them all right.

Mr. FITZPATRICK moved second reading of Bill (No. 147) to amend the Acts relating to Naturalization and Aliens. He said : As I explained on the first reading, this is intended to meet a difficulty in the province of Quebec. Under the law application must be made to the circuit court of the district. This court sits at the chief place in the district and in addition at other places. The clerks .in the circuit court, in order, I suppose, to avoid unnecessary labour, contend that applications for naturalization must Mr. SPROULE.
be made at the chief place or shire town, and cannot be made at other places where the court sits. Since introducing this Bill, it has attracted attention in the province of Manitoba, and I have a letter from the exchief justice of that province, Judge Killam, in which he suggests an amendment of a similar nature applicable to that province. Let me read his letter :
Winnipeg, 9th July, 1904.
Dear Sir,-Observing that you have introduced a Bill to amend the Naturalization Act, I desire again to call your attention to some points which I mentioned to you some time ago, when I was Chief Justice of Manitoba.
By section 11 of the Act, Revised Statutes Canada, chapter 113, the naturalization certificate is to he presented (in Manitoba) to the Court of Queen's (now King's) Bench during its sitting in the eounty in which the alien resides, or to the court of assize, &e., or to the county court of such county.
There are now no courts of assize and ' nisi prius ' in the province. There are sittings of the Court of King's Bench for commercial and jury trials twice each year in each judicial district (which, under the interpretation clause is the * county ').
There are weekly sittings of the Court of King's Bench at Winnipeg for non-jury trials, also weekly sittings for motions and legal arguments. These have always been considered sittings within the Naturalization Act and many naturalization certificates have been brought up and read at these.
At times, at trial sittings, many parties are present as witnesses. But often at these, and usually at the other sittings there are only a few lawyers.
The reading of such certificates at these sittings gives no publicity and is often a great nuisance to the judge, the officials and those having business before the court.
I would suggest that all such certificates be presented in the county courts. This affords a far better chance of securing publicity among the neighbours of the alien, the sole object of such reading.
Chief Justice Killman sends me a draft-clause which he suggests as a substitute for that relating to Manitoba, which is as follows :
Said section 11 is further amended by striking out line 20 to 26 both inclusive and substituting the following :-' In Manitoba to the county court having jurisdiction where the alien resides or if there be no county court having jurisdiction there, then to some other county court in the province.
This amendment I will move when the Bill reaches committee.

If I understand the object of this amendment of the law with regard to Quebec, then, taking the example given by the hon. minister (Mr. Fitzpatrick) the alien may be naturalized on applying to the circuit court in any town in which the circuit court sits, and is not obliged to apply at the sitting in the chef lieu, or chief town of the district. I think

that is all right. But I would call the attention of the hon. minister to the second clause which makes the law retroactive, from and including 13th August, 1903. I .suppose my hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) will give us some explanation and reasons for the introduction of this retroactive .clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not the statute here, and cannot refer to Jt, but the object of this second section is to give effect to any naturalization certificates which may have been issued in the interval by some of the circuit courts sitting outside the chef lieu.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
To explain my own position, I may say that I have never entertained any doubt that these petitions could be presented at the circuit court sitting anywhere in the district. But the difficulty is that the clerks of the court, over whom we have no jurisdiction, to save themselves the labour of these certificates, for which they get no remuneration, insist on the
work being done at the headquarters of the court.

If the House will bear with me, I would call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that retroactive legislation is objectionable in principle. I suppose I can get the assurance of my hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) that it does not interfere with any action of law pending before the court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot give that because I do not know. We might protect that point by amending the clause to provide that it shall not interfere with any question now in litigation. But I cannot say that there is no litigation.
This, of course, is objectionable on the face of it-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I quite agree.
And possibly it would be better to add some clause such as the minister suggests. I do not know that I quite gather how this particular date of 13th August, 1903, was arrived at.

This was the day on which the Act of last session was assented to. Of course, I am not contending that the present law ought to be changed. I simply pointed out that where it was printed in the old Act ' circuit ' in ' which the alien residesf it v*rcis printed in tiie A.ct of lB.st year ' district.' The petitions I referred to, presented last year to the judge of the circuit court under this law, he would not receive, because he said they ought to be presented at the chef lieu.
The answer is perfectly satisfactory. The date is that on which the Act of last session became law.

Bill (No. 154) to amend chapter 61 of the statutes of 1903, respecting the Revised Statutes of Canada-Mr. Fitzpatrick-was lead the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 2,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 4 of the present statute reads as follows:
The Governor in Council, after such deposit of the said last mentioned roll, may by proclamation declare.
There is only one roll, therefore the use of the words ' last mentioned ' Is unnecessary.

I should think that this is a proper amendment. I have not specially examined the statute of last year, but I may say to the hon. Minister of Justice that under a somewhat similar statute in the province of Nova Scotia a very curious condition has arisen. Perhaps he may have heard something of it. It seems that a roll in exact conformity with the report of the commissioners with certain additions and corrections taken from the statutes of the same year was prepared ? In the margin of that some person had pencilled a word. It had been in the former statute, but it had been omitted from that statute by subsequent legislation. The statute of the province providing for the roll was to the effect that after the roll was prepared by the commissioners and after it was printed it

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: should toe signed by the Governor and the provincial secretary and that it should be regarded as the original roll. When it was printed it was printed with the inclusion of this pencilled word in the margin and the result was that very important litigation arose which was recently determined by the Supreme Court of Canada. In the litigation another point arose which is worthy of consideration at the present time; that is to say whether or not the printed roll so provided for by the statute and signed by the government and provincial secretary would have the same force and effect as the roll of parliament, or whether it could be controverted by evidence which could not be introduced to controvert. If the roll of parliament as finally signed and verified by the officers of parliament and the Governor himself could be shown by the most indisputable evidence to differ in any respect from the legislation' as it had passed the committees of this House or had pased the third reading of this House and the Senate, you could not controvert it by any evidence of that kind because it imputes absolute verity. I would think that, taking every precaution to make sure that the roll shall be absolutely correct, it is desirable in this statute, if it has not already been done, to make it absolutely clear that the roll so signed by the proper authorities named in this statute shall impute the same verity and shall be as binding and conclusive as the roll of parliament itself would be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not quite sure whether these amendments have been suggested as a result of the difficulty which occurred in the province of Nova Scotia to which my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) has referred, but I may say that these amendments have been prepared as a result of a report made to me by three gentlemen who went over this roll and who were appointed a sub-committee by the commission for that purpose. These gentlemen were Mr. Newcombe, Mr. Roscoe, and Mr. Sirois. These three careful and painstaking gentlemen having examined the roll have suggested these amendments.
How far have they got with the revision ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I had expected to be called upon to make a statement when I brought down my estimates in connection with the item which I will have to submit to the House. Then I will be able to give all the details to my hon. friend, but I may say that the work is very far advanced and that I think early within the next year the whole matter will be disposed of.
On section 3,
What is the effect of that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In one section they called it 'the last roll' and in the other ' the amended roll.'
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

House in Committee of Supply.
Welland canal-electric lighting and power plant, $100,000.

['I think the clause was somewhat hastily drawn, and it was thought well after by the Senate Committee and after consultation with the Railway Department it was thought well to make this amendment.\nMotion agreed to and amendments concurred in.']
I notice that under the contract the government takes 500 horsepower and it may be extended to 700.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. R. EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
Yes, if we require it.
I do not think the original arrangement with the Lincoln Company was by tender, but tenders have been called for all the materials required.
What materials do you require ?
They only supply the power under that contract, but we have to install the plant ; and everything is included in this vote.
What is the price per horse-power ?
This contract is for the supply of horse-power only 1
Yes.
Last session the government explained that the supplies for the electric plant would be obtained by tender.
That has been done. Mr. BLAIN. Who were the tenderers ?

The Canadian General Electric Company, the Packard Electric Company, the Canadian Westinghouse Company ; there were quite a number. All the materials were not purchased from the one concern. Some prices were lower on some articles than on others, and I selected from the tenders the articles that were quoted at the lowest prices.
What will the total construction of the electric plant, when complete, cost ?
The estimate given by 'Mr. Parke, the electrical expert, of the lighting and the power plant is $250,000. It will not be exceeded I understand.
When will it be completed ?
It should have been completed this month, but these companies have failed to come to time.

Is the government under any obligation to the contractors for power,
in case the plant is not constructed by a certain time ?
No, when we are ready to take the horse-power we will pay for it.
What horse-power do you require for moving the gates, &c., in contradistinction to the power used in generating the electricity for the lights ?
We require hardly 400 horse-power for the lights alone and the balance of the 500 will be required for the gates and bridges.
How many lights have you ?
About 500 lights of 2,000 candle-power requiring about three-quarters of a horse-power to a light.
What length is the canal that you are lighting ?
Twenty-seven miles is the length of the canal and we are lighting it throughout.
Does this complete the expense on the Welland canal ?

Yes, this completes the improvements. We have to take out the centre piers of the bridges that cross the canal. In the interests of navigation that becomes necessary. We are not doing that all at one time, but year by year as it becomes necessary we will do so. There is one in contemplation now at St. Catharines known as the Niagara street bridge. The centre pier will have to be removed and the present bridge replaced by a larger and heavier structure.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to the question suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) as to Whether this will complete the expenditure in regard to the lighting on the Welland canal. I have been endeavouring to impress on the minister and I would like to impress on parliament this one fact that the proper thing for the government to do is to put in their own electrical plant and not to make any contract with any company. That is the cheapest way to do it ; there is water going to waste on the Welland canal in very large quantities. The government can install its own electrical plant, light the Welland canal and open and operate lock gates and bridges very much more cheaply in my opinion, and I think in the opinion of experts, than they are doing it under the contract which they have entered into now, although the contract which has been entered into is an exceedingly reasonable one so far as the prices are concerned. In view of what the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) has just stated. I beg to suggest that the proper thing to be done is for the government to install its own electrical

plant and use its own water-power for lighting the canal and operating the locks and bridges.

That was the feature of it which attracted my attention. If we have power going to waste, why should we pay for power from_an outside corporation? The power we are paying for is water-power. I understand that the government put in their own plant but pay the company for power. What power is it if not water-power that they are paying for ?

I suppose that the hon. gentleman from Welland is aware that this contract is for ten years. Is it not a fact that power is becoming cheaper from time to time in this district, and does not my hon. friend think that it is rather an unwise move to enter into a ten year contract for power of this kind when the price of power is being reduced very rapidly ? The plan advocated by the hon. gentleman (Mr. German), namely that the government operate the whole thing, might be very much cheaper he says and for that reason I think that entering into a ten year contract is not a good move. I think we could do better.

Why enter into a contract with an outside company for power, if we have water going to waste which contains all the power we require ? Why not use the water going to waste on the Welland canal, install a plant there, operate the locks and bridges and canal and light it as well, in that way.
That might be done very rapidly but it would involve a large expenditure of money in order to utilize that power.
How could it ?

It is not something lying there to be availed of at any moment. For the utilization of that water-power a mechanical arrangement is required and the expense is considerable ; I do not know how much. However, be that as it may, it stands in this position that a contract was entered into and we are now under contract to take so much power from the Lincoln Company, and we have to furnish a certain equipment along the line of the Welland canal in order to utilize the power that we thus secure from that company.

If you use your own power you would have to do no more than you are doing to-day. If you have the water penned up and the requisite pressure it simply requires a wheel to bring it into operation. Ail you would require then to connect that with your machinery is a water wheel. Every one knows that that is not a very expensive item. Then you have the power, and if I understand correctly you are installing your own dynamos and other Mr. GERMAN.
plant. Since the government must do that, why should they pay $14 per horse-power when they have so much power going to waste ? All they need do is to install the plant and utilize that power. You would then have your own power and would not be bound by any contract and could take advantage of every improvement to cheapen it.

I do not know as to the relative cost of furnishing the waterpower and purchasing it, but I am informed that the government, if they wanted to utilize the water-power along the Welland canal, would have to spend more than they are paying this company.
Have you an engineer's report to that effect ?
No.
Then that is just mere rumour.
It is more that a rumour, it is a statement.
By whom ?
From the department.
That statement must be based on knowledge.

However, the contract is let, and that is only a statement with reference to the cost. It may or may not be correct. I certainly cannot vouch for it. But I can say that $14 per horse-power is certainly a very reasonable figure, as water-powers are leased in Canada to-day.

I may tell the hon. minister that I am interested in a contract for the supply of electric power, not only waterpower but the electric current as well, for $8 per horse-power, and we carry that five miles by wire.
Where is that ?

Right where I live. That is a very reasonable rate, and it show's that where water is plentiful power can be supplied very cheaply. The minister says the contract is let and of course there is a vested right, but I am arguing antecedent to the letting of the contract. I am contending that business prudence would have sug-gester the necessity of making ample inquiry and securing sufficient data to satisfy the minister that the power could not be furnished cheaper by using the water that is going to waste in the canal.
What is the date of the contract ?
5th of December is the date of the Order in Council.

1st of July, I think. The only point in this discussion is whether it would be cheaper for the government to generate their own power. That I think

we must admit. You are furnishing everything outside the power, and since you have to go to so much expenditure in furnishing plant, why not complete your plant and furnish your own power ? You would then have control for all time to come instead of being in the hands of a company. I am strongly of the opinion of the hon. member for Welland that that would be the right step to take in view of the enormous waterpower in the neighbourhood.

Personally the matter has not come under my notice as to whether it would be advisable or not to utilize that water-power, but it does occur to me that it could not be utilized without the expenditure of a very considerable sum in addition to what we are spending. I did not even make personal inquiry to ascertain whether there is ample power along the canal, because there has been no occasion for me to do so. And I am therefore not in a position to give an opinion.
How much have you let in that canal to outsiders ?
There is a great deal under lease, and the leases go over many years. Water-powers are being applied for.
Is there not still power, over and above what is leased, sufficient to do all the lighting of the canal and operate the gates and bridges ?
I think there could be some leased, but I have not had occasion to make inquiry, for the simple reason that we entered into a contract in 1902.
There is an excuse for the minister that he was not responsible at the time.
I am not relieving myself of responsibility, but am simply drawing attention to the fact that personally I have not felt called upon to make inquiry.
If the minister is assuming responsibility for what his predecessors did, he is responsible for their mistakes and blunders as well as successes.
Certainly.

We are selling power, I am told, in many cases at a merely nominal figure. Look at the power we sold on the [DOT]Cornwall canal. I venture toi say that there is over 1,000 horse-power, probably 2,000, on that canal, and we are selling it at $1,000 a year. That would not amount to SI a horse-power, yet we are buying it back at $63 horse-power. Can that be called good management ? What is the essential cost of the development of power ? It must be developed by steam or water-power. All through the country the great requisite is water-power, because then you save the cost of fuel and machinery for the generation of steam. Wherever you have water pent up you can generate power very cheaply. And it is a permanent power. We nave that power there, and we could sell it, or we would use it to generate electrical energy. But we lease the right to others tor a nominal figure, and then we buy back at a considerable figure the power which they generate by using the opportunities that we have leased to them. I am not saying that the price paid by the government is exorbitant; frankly, I do not think it is. But we could produce that power for our own use if we provided the proper means. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) says that it would be very costly machinery. The hon. minister is mistaken. Where you have the water already stored up, all you need is a pen-stock and a wheel. This will produce the power, and you can use that power to run a dynamo, a saw-mill or any other machinery. I contend that it does not show good business management for the head of a department to allow power to go to waste, and, at the same time, buy power from outsiders. And, especially, this does not show good business management when a contract is made for ten years to pay a certain rate per horse-power. No matter what inventions may be made to develop power cheaply, we are'compelled to pay,the same price under the contract. And if we find fault we are told that contracts are sacred, and, even if we can get the service at a cheaper rate, we must continue to pay the price agreed upon. I contend that the department should have had one of its engineers ascertain what power is available ; and, if enough power was going to waste to work the locks and bridges and generate electricity to light the canal, that power should have been used, rather than take power from an outsider under such a contract as this. In this case there seems ample evidence that we could supply the power at a rate much less than that we are paying. To say that is to say that the minister is not doing his duty in not having the investigation made to learn the best means of utilizing that power.
The Lincoln Company, of course, sell their power. But they had to spend a very large sum of money in order to develop that power.
The hon. Minister should not insist that it requires a large expenditure to utilize this power, now that the water is pent up.
The power has to be developed, and that means a permanent investment.

What does the hon. minister mean by ' developed ' ? The first requisite in the making of a water-power is a dam, and that is often a very expensive work. But in this case the dams are all

made. The water is now running in the sluice-ways. It is only necessary to put in a wheel to utilize the power.

But it means putting up buildings and installing machinery. I understand it requires a very large expenditure to develop water-power, and the mere fact that you have the water does not mean that you have power-you must harness it.

But the main expense of harnessing is the making of a dam, and that work is already done. Common sense must tell the minister, as it tells me, that when a company is furnishing power to the government the company must receive interest on its investment, and that the government is paying that interest in the price it pays for the power.
I admit that I am not an authority on these points. I am glad of suggestions from my hon. friends.
Then if the minister is not an authority, why does he not
I am modest enough to admit that I am not an authority, but my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) perhaps is not modest enough to admit the same concerning himself.

The difficulty is that the minister admits too much. Of course, we do not expect the minister now to know everything about his department. But he has a competent staff, and they are there for the purpose of giving him information. And I am very strongly of opinion that no minister should come down here and ask the House to vote money -without proper information. There is no excuse for ignorance. If he has not been in his office long enough to learn it himself, his staff will furnish it for him. Does not the company that furnishes this power get that power from the water in the canal ? If so, they must put in the necessary machinery to develop the power, and on their investment they must receive interest. I do not think it requires such an enormous amount of capital. In the section in which I live there are immense water-powers, but to utilize them is an expensive matter, because in every case you must first build a dam. But once the dam is made the putting in of the machinery is an insignificant thing. I believe, and I think the committee feel, that the minister should take steps to find if he could not utilize the power now going to waste and at the same time save money to the country. I am not finding fault with the amount he is paying if he must buy the power. But if we can use the power that we now own and so avoid paying to somebody else, it should be an advantage to have this power harnessed.

It seems that there has been no calculation made as to whether we can get power more cheaply by utilizing the Mr. SPROULE.
water that is going to waste in the canai. I do not call that good business management ; in fact, I think it is bad business management. The minister should make the same inquiry that a wise business man would make in such a case ; and I think that that might have been done before now.

The contract price for this power is $14 per horse-power. At Niagara Falls, New York, manufacturing companies are paying from $25 to $30 per horsepower for electric power delivered on the spot. There are three companies carrying on operations to develop electric power on the Canadian side at Niagara Falls. It is said that when they have finished the work of development which is now going on, which, I think, will be this fall-one of them, the Canadian Niagara Power Company, by December, at any rate-you will not be able to get power from them for less than from $15 to $20 per horse-power. Under those circumstances, it can hardly be said that the price charged the government by the Lincoln Company is too high. I quite agree, however, and must again insist, that the proper thing for the government to do is to develop the power itself. .
I quite agree with the idea that power should be given to the government to develop this power itself. I had an opportunity of discussing this matter with the late Minister of Railways and suggested to him that the government should put in plant and develop power rather than give the contract to a company ; but he thought that at that particular time it was more advisable to enter into the contract for ten years. We know that this very company has been urging strenuously on the government that the contract should be extended ; as a matter of fact people interested in the company have spoken to me about it, asking me if I would use my influence, if I had any, with the department to obtain a further extension of this contract.
They would like it for a hundred years.

No doubt. The price of powter will be lower, but I doubt if it will be lower within the life of the contract. I think $14 per horse-power during the life of this contract is probably about as low a figure as you could get power for. I would not be in favour of extending the contract, and I think that if the government can see its way to put in plant of its own and utilize the water that is going to waste on the Welland canal to develop power which will operate all the locks and bridges and furnish light on the canal, it would be the best thing to do in the public interest. I have made that statement before, and I am prepared to stand by it, because I do not think it can be controverted. As far as price is concerned, I think the price that is being paid now is reasonable. The hon.

member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) asked how much power was being used by manufacturers on the Welland canal. I venture to say there is 100,000 horse-power, probably more than that.
Going to waste.
It is not wasted, it is in the canal.

It is practically wasted as long as it is not used.
|Mr. GERMAN. We must have water there in order to have a canal.
Would not the water run on just the same even though the power was not used ?

The hon. gentleman says it does not cost much to put in machinery. I can tell him that it costs an enormous sum of money to put in machinery. Go to the Westinghouse Company and ask them what is the cost of dynamos per horse-power necessary to light and operate the Welland canal.
I thought the minister said they put in the dynamos and the plant themselves.
I was mistaken with respect to that, I had not the contract before me.
As to the price of power, we paid that much for horse-power per annum already, before the contract.
It is $14 per horse-power per year.
But that was not in use during the full year.
By the contract it is only paid proportionately, we do not have to pay for the whole year.
Would the minister tell us about how much it will cost the government to supply the power for electric lighting and the horse-power, separately ?
The estimated cost of installing the arc light system ?

No, I am asking, when the $10,000 plant for both electric lighting and power is completed, what will be the total cost to the government of the power to be used for the gates, and the cost of the electric lighting separately.

As I said to my hon. friend, the government expect to spend fully $250,000, and after expending that sum we will have a lighting plant and a power plant. Then we will be called upon to pay after that for the power generated by the Lincoln Company at the rate of $14 per horse-power.
Per annum ?

At that rate per annum, in proportion to the length of time in each year that it is used.
iMr. BLAIN. The hon. gentleman has already told us that. What I am asking is, how much do the government expect it will cost to operate these two distinct plants when the work is done. The hon. gentleman has told us $14 per horse-power. 1 suppose the government will have some estimate made as to how much it will cost per year to supply the power.
The cost will not exceed $7,000. We hope it will be within that sum.

Before the Orders of the Day were called, I asked the right hon. the Prime Minister if he could give the House ..any information with respect to the military situation at Sydney. There have been reports in the newspapers that the militia who had been sent on duty to that town have been withdrawn, and their places taken by the regular military force of the Dominion. It has also been stated that a warship has been sent round from Halifax. I would like to know from the Minister of [DOT] Militia what the facts are in connection with the trouble down there ?

speakeroldname: Sir FREDERICK BORDEN (Minister of Militia and Gefence).
speechtext: Under the provisions of the statute, three magistrates of Sydney, Cape Breton, one of them being the stipendiary magistrate of the town, made a request upon the district officer commanding at Halifax for assistance. The district officer at Halifax called out, in the first instance, the local militia,' which was not found to be adequate ; and later on he sent 200 men, I think, from the city of Halifax. As the difficulties continued, and appeared likely to continue for some time longer, and as these men were employed in Halifax in various ways and their absence was causing inconvenience, the district officer commanding asked headquarters to lend 100 men of the permanent force to go to Sydney and replace the active militia so that they might return to their homes and their work.
How many of the active militia were on duty ?

About 200, I think. This was agreed to, upon condition that the money, necessary to pay the cost of transportation and all expenses, was deposited in the bank at Sydney to the credit of the Receiver General. Upon that being done, and the department being informed of the fact through the bank-and I may say the money was deposited by the three magistrates already mentioned-the troops were allowed to go. and are there now, under these conditions. With reference to the warship, I have no information at all. I was not aware

that a warship was there. I do know, however, that it is the custom of warships, British warships and others, to call occasionally at the port of Sydney. I presume this was merely one of the occasional calls.

I am very glad to have the explanation of the minister in this matter. When the announcement was made that the regulars were being sent and that a warship was proceeding to Sydney, I feared the situation was more serious than it really is.

My hon. friend from East Urey (Mr. Sproulej seemed to take exception to the purchase of power for lighting and operating the gates on the Welland canal, and he seemed to be of the opinion that the government might have utilized the powers which they have on the canal. It is well known that I was not personally cognizant of the transaction at the time, but I find on looking into the matter that the expert employed by the department at that time, in a report presented in November, 1902, sets forth his views. I will read this report to the committee. The expert is Mr. Roderick J. Parke, consulting electrical engineer of Toronto. The report is as follows :
Ottawa, Out., Nov. 2Sth, 1902.

subtopic: ELECTRIC LIGHTING CONTRACT FOR WELLAND CANAL.
ELECTRIC LIGHTING CONTRACT FOR WELLAND CANAL.
speechtext:
Blair,
Minister of Railways and Canals,
Ottawa.
Sir,-In accordance with your instructions I have examined and read the correspondence in the matter of the proposal by the Lincoln Electric Light and Power Company, Limited, of St. Catharines, Ont., to supply electrical power to the Dominion of Canada for the operation of electric arc lights along the canal and of electric motors at the various locks, bridges, shops, and so forth, on the canal, and I beg to submit my report herewith :-
The company propose to supply electrical power at the rate of fourteen dollars per horse-power for such amount of power as may be required to supply light for about 400 enclosed arc lamps of 2,000 candle power each, from the opening until the close of navigation, beginning May 1st, 1903, each year for ten years.
They further propose to supply power for about 100 lamps, all the year round for the water watch, presumably 2,000 candle power lamps for this service, and I further presume that the power required for the said 100 lamps is not to be added to the amount of power required for the total number of lamps (arc) in use during the season of navigation.
They further propose to supply any further power that may be called for in the future for operating lock gates and bridges and workshops at any time at the same rate per horse-power, namely, $14.

During my stay at the Soo, a boat was sunk, some place east of the Soo and a blockade of shipping ensued ; I presume that 100 to 150 vessels of all sizes and shapes were tied up there but not one of them came to the Canadian side. I discussed the question with the people there, and I was told that the boats could not land on the Canadian side owing to lack of water. Yet the hon. member f<M' Welland (Mr. German) says that Canadian boats can buy supplies on the Canadian side. They cannot, because if they do they have to put the supplies on the ferry boat and take tSiem across to the American side where they will be met by a customs officer as I was, and be obliged to pay duty. They could only put the supplies on board without paying duty while the boats were passing through the Canadian lock, but if another boat came along they would be unable to tie up long enough to do that, so that practically it is impossible for Canadian boats to take on supplies at the Canadian Soo, or to land passengers there with comfort. On my return I brought the matter before the House at the first opportunity but I presume that affairs are in the same position to-day as they were then. No boat of any size can

land on tlie Canadian side of the river owing to the shallowness of the water. The old government built a canal and had it about completed when this government came in, but the approaches and docking facilities to-day remain just as they were then.

It will get a great deal of benefit from it, not only' the direct advantage of affording means of transportation to a large class of people along the line of the canal which traverses a farming district which in many parts is unsurpassed, but it will be of great incidental advantage to the people by affording direct competition with the railway and so reducing and controlling rates. In this I think the hon. minister will be ready to agree with me. Therefore, I think there can be no excuse that the government could urge or that the government would be disposed to urge for not taking this work in hand as a definite work to be completed within a reasonable date. 500,000	in it now and within ten years we will have, according to the present rate of progress, $3,000,000"or $4,0000.000 more so that it will then cost us about $300,000 a year in interest. Why, my dear man, what are you doing ? For half an hour you talked unmitigated nonsense which you did not believe yourself, and which no one listening to you believed.
Why don't you let the vote pass if you are in favour of the canal.

No intelligent man would have a doubt in his mind as to where the outlet of that canal is going to be. If you want it to be of any benefit you know where it is going to be, and if you were not humbugging the people and playing to the gallery you would state so openly. I do not care about the expenditure of
money in East Northumberland
You are not voicing the opinion of the people of East Northumberland in that.

I am voicing the opinion of the people of East Northumberland, when I say that their desire is to have the public money expended where it will be for the best advantage of all Canada. We are not local in our ideas. Do you understand that ? I suppose it is incomprehensible to certain of these gentlemen opposite, how people can stand on a plane so high as that. The ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Haggart) is here, and he can tell that I always insisted that the public money should be spent in the best interests of Canada. I knew that if the money for this canal were wisely expended the canal would go down the Trent route. It is two-thirds way across the riding I have the honour to represent. It is navigable to Healey's Falls and with a lift-lock like that at Peterborough, it would bring it down to the level of the waters of the Trent, and then it would develop water-power all along that route. I want to tell the Postmaster General if he doesn't know it, that there is a bay below Healey's Falls, and from Chisholm's Rapids westward there are ten miles of navigable water, so that it is not all canal. If his estimate is right that there are eighteen miles to complete, then deduct the ten miles, and you have only eight miles of canal to Trenton. Does the minister think that he can locate the entrance of this canal at Port Hope when he knows that in the fall of the year the barges could not live on Lake Ontario, from the harbour of Port Hope to the harbour of PresquTle. I may not live to see the canal completed, but I will live as long as I can and, I hope to see the Postmaster General out of power and then he will not be able to humbug the electors in talking about Port Hope or Cobourg or anywhere else in order to catch votes. These hon. gentlemen opposite know as well as I do that the outlet must be on the Bay of Quintd where the barges can take the inland waters, and bring their cargoes to Quebec and Montreal without transhipment. I do not want the Postmaster General to leave the impression that I am opposed to that canal going to Trenton. I thought that question was settled, and I believe it is settled, and the Postmaster General knows deep down in his heart that he is only humbugging the electors when he talks about it going to Port Hope or Cobourg.

My hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) pretends to be very anxious to have this canal completed to the town of Trenton. He belongs to a party that began that work in 1880. They were in that office from that time until 1896, a period of sixteen years. The total cost of that canal would be, I suppose, $10,000,000. In sixteen years they had not built one-
