twelfth part of that canal, in sixteen years they had not accomplished one-twelftli of the work. At the rate of progress they were making, it would have taken nearly two hundred years to have completed that work, and the hon. member would tell this House that he hopes to live to see it completed. The only chance he ever had of realizing that hope was that the enterprise should be put in the hands of an enterprising government. That happened to be the good fortune of the canal in 1896. My hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) says that he never gave a thought to the Trenton route. I would have thought that, as representing Hast Northumberland, he would have given thought to it continually, would have been ever alert to guard the interests of East Northumberland and to see that the canal came by that route.
I knew it was settled.
You knew it was settled ?
Yes.

How did he learn that it was settled ? I have asked his late leader, the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, if it had been settled in that way by the Trenton route. What answer did I get ? The hon. gentleman made the confession that he favoured the Trenton route, but he receded from that in a moment, and my hon. friend from East Northumberland backed him up.
No, 1 did not.
The Debates will show. I say that the hon. gentleman backed him up in withdrawing any expression he had given in favour of the Trenton route.
No, I did not.

And I had occasion to point out that my hon. friend was not doing justice to East Northumberland.
The attitude of the government in regard to the enterprise is perfectly plain. It is quite true that certain engineering reports have been made in favour of the Trenton route, and it may be that those reports are well founded and that the balance of argument is wholly in favour of the Trenton route. But inasmuch as a very influential section of the country has asked to have another route considered, I may ask my hon. friend if it is not only fair that their request should be listened to and that full consideration should be given to their contention ? My hon. friend has as much as said so himself at this moment, because he says he is not wedded to any route ; he rises above local Considerations. No pent up Utica for him, and the money is to be expended where it will do the most good If a more thorough inquiry should show that it would be best to adopt the Port 2181
Hope route, my hon. friend will be found standing up here supporting the Port Hope route. WEI he not ? He has made great professions of virtue, he is not a partisan in the sense that he would have the money misapplied. He is in favour of the Port Hope route, according to his statements here to-night, if it can be shown to be the better route, and therefore he, like others, is asking us to consider the whole situation and not to reach a conclusion after only a partial consideration of the question. So we now have a statesman instead of the former mere local politician from .East Northumberland. He is willing to support this route if it is necessary for the benefit of Canada as a whole. I compliment him on the high stand he has taken. However, if he would really stand the test when it comes to submitting this to the decision of a final tribunal, time alone will tell. In the meantime the government propose to proceed expeditiously in the completion of this enterprise, as rapidly as the circumstances of this country will admit. The hon. gentleman protests against our spending money, and at the same time says he is anxious for the completion of the canal. We are told its completion will cost $4,000,000 or $5,000,000. Can we build it without money ? The hon. gentleman protests against the expenditure of money necessary for the completion of the canal ; therefore, he must be opposed to the completion of the canal. He cannot take all these inconsistent positions in the same breath. The country is committed to the completion of the canal : the government regards it as an enterprise of great promise, which is entitled to be completed as rapidly as circumstances will warrant. That is our attitude, and to that attitude we propose to adhere.
The Postmaster General has continued on the same line, trying to make a little cheap political capital out of this great question.
Never dreamt of such a thing.
And has put words in my mouth which I never uttered, and which he knows I never uttered. I am not going to allow him or any one else to say that I said certain things which I did not say.
What did you not say ?

I would (think you would be above interrupting me. You should play the part of a gentleman anyway in the discussion. I never said that I was in favour of the Port Hope route. I said that I believed that that question was settled, and therefore I had not given it a thought, because I thought that any sensible government would decide on the route that had been decided on for seventy years past. That is what I thought, and I think in my own mind to-day that that question is

settled just as firmly in the mind or the present government as in the mind of any previous government, only they want to make a little cheap notoriety out of the matter.	*
Nothing of the kind.

You can shake your head ; I do not think there is much in it, and it is easy to shake it; hut I am not going to allow you to put words in my mouth and put me in a false position. I will repeat what I said. I never was asking the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals to spend money in my riding because I represented that riding. I thought the money would be expended when the proper time came, and I would wish to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to the statement that he has made, that he is going to complete this canal as rapidly as the circumstances of the country will warrant. Will he not allow the same latitude to the previous government as to the present government ? This government is asking the House to vote $70,000,000, and should not the previous government have shown the same consideration for the interests of the country when it was in power with only $37,000,000 of revenue ? I pointed out to him what we were doing with that $35,000,000. We were deepening and completing the canals, but the present government is doing no such thing. All public work, so far as canals are concerned, is now centred on the Trent canal, and although the Postmaster General tells as that the government is so anxious to complete this canal expeditiously, yet there is only a paltry $100,000 out of that $70,-C00,000 voted for that purpose. I cannot see how you have-I was going to say the cheek, but perhaps that would not be parliamentary-but I cannot see how you can stand up before this committee and tell the country that you are anxious to go on with this work when you are voting a total of $70,000,000, of which only $100,000 is to carry on this work, and then make a great plea on account of that expenditure. The contracts were all made by the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, and you have carried them out. I think when you think the matter over and see what an exhibition you have made of yourself, you will feel sad.

If you are anxious for the completion of the canal vote the money. The hon. gentleman is here obstructing the passage of this vote ; if he is so anxious to have the canal completed why should he not have the money voted ? If we have this amount of difficulty to get a paltry $100,000, what would the difficulty be with a larger sum ?
I was not objecting to it.
The country will understand how interested he is when he will not allow us to get the estimates through for this paltry sum.

If the Postmaster General was not so willing and anxious to make political capital, and to make himself conspicuous, coming to the rescue of the Minister of Railways and Canals when it was not necessary, we would not have had all this debate.

I have just a few words to say to the hon. the Postmaster General, because I think he has been making rather an unfair attack on my hon. friend from East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane). The Postmaster General complains that the previous government did not proceed rapidly enough with the construction of this public work, and compared the progress which the present government have made with that made by the late government from 1880 to 1896. But let me, Sir, draw attention to this fact, that from 1880 to 1896- and I believe the Postmaster General had the honour of a seat in this House all that time-the opposition of that day made every effort to obstruct this public work, and the hon. gentleman himself was one of the movst prominent in that obstruction. If there were delays during those sixteen years the government of that day could not be held responsible.
Why not ?

Because every dollar that the late government succeeded in obtaining from parliament to expend on that work was practically, owing to the obstruction of the then opposition, like drawing teeth, to use a common expression.
You had an overwhelming majority.
Yes; but day after day the time of the committee was wasted in obstructing that public work, and every effort of the opposition was directed to prevent its being proceeded with.
No.

We know the tactics that were resorted to by hon. gentlemen opposite in those days. Why, the present government lias a very easy road compared with what the late government had in more matters than one. In the construction of public works they were opposed at every turn ; and when they did succeed in getting a few hundred thousand dollars, they were hounded from one end of the country to the other for their extravagance. Those hon. gentlemen opposite who constitute the remnant of the old opposition were largely responsible for the delays that occurred, and therefore it ill becomes] the Postmaster General-who was one of the foremost of those who denounced this public work as

worthless and as being constructed for (political purposes-to now taunt the late government with delay. I do not live in the neighbourhood of that canal, I do not pretend to know the topography of that country, I am not a judge as to whether Trenton or Port Hope is the proper outlet, the matter is one in which I am not personally interested ; but I have no doubt that had the late government remained in power, they v\ould have determined long before this what route was best in the interests of the country, irrespective of politics. I hope that the Postmaster General, now that he has had his memory refreshed, will withdraw some of the charges he has preferred against the late government for delays. The former government spent very considerable sums in preparing to push this work through. In 1887 they spent more money on that canal than the present government spent in 1899. From 1896 to 1903 more money was spent on the canal each year, except one, than was spent in the previous years. But the reason is evident. Hon. gentlemen on this side are patriotic. We believe in having a public work, which is of great advantage to the country, completed. We assist the government in these matters instead of giving it the bitterest opposition. I notice also that two of the contracts which, I understand, are jus|t about completed, if not already completed, were let by the late government. They were given by the predecessors of the hon. gentlemen now in power-one of them in 1895 and the other in May, 1896. So that the late government should not only have credit for the money they did spend, but also for having pushed that work forward even to the very dying days of that administration. I think there is as much credit due to the ex-Minister of Railways, who gave out these contracts, as to the present government, which carried them to completion. We are not offering to the present government the factious opposition which hon. gentlemen opposite, when on this side, offered the late government. We act like men who take a keen interest in the affairs of the country, and hon. gentlemen opposite, instead of taunting us with the results of their obstruction in the past, should give us credit for helping them to expedite business in the present.

I desire to say a word on this question. I think that a member from a province in which the canal is not situated will probably be in a better position to voice the sentiment of Canada than one directly interested in the work. I want to say here that it gives me the greatest pleasure to support the building of this water-way. Ever since I have entered this House I have endeavoured to inculcate the principle that we should not vijew any public question from a narrow provincial standpoint. I have gone so far as to say that we should be the last to advocate expenditure in our own particular province.
That should be left to people outside, because the members themselves should regard all the provinces as but one country, and should be as interested in the development of every other portion of Canada as they are in the little spot in which they happen to live. I am now in a position to justify the stand I have taken ever since entering this House. When 1 received the invitation to visit Peterborough, I made up my mind to go and see the opening of this great public work. I went, I may say, in fear and trembling, because I believe that if there is a stain on the escutcheon of the Conservative party, it is the Trent canal.
I concur absolutely in what my hon. friend from Haiton (Mr. Henderson) and my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) have said, namely, that no work was ever more represented by gentlemen constituting Her Majesty's opposition as a low political job than the building of the Trent canal.
I live in Nova Scotia. I was not familiar with the location of the Trent Valley canal. I knew nothing about the possibilities of the water-ways of that section. And so, I, and others in Nova Scotia like me, had to take the word of members of parliament. We, in Nova Scotia, had learned to respect members of parliament. We had men to represent us like, for instance, Hon. Mr. Ross, who, though he differs from me politically, wouid be fair in this discussion of a public question. He is a strong Liberal, and, if he ever went wrong, it was when he was swayed by that unholy passion. But, we were accustomed to public men who would fairly represent the interests of the country, and we could not believe that any public man would prostitute his position in the House of Commons, to misrepresent a work that was calculated to be a benefit to his country. I went to Peterborough, the other day, with fear and trembling. When 1 received an invitation from the government, I thought, at last, the government was to show the country the extraordinary character of this work. I fancied they would say : We found this scheme, which was a piece of political debauchery, only half completed ; we have done the best we could with it; we are in possession of the record, and we want to lay before you the jobbery of the Conservative party in connection with this work. So, as I say, I went there in fear and trembling. The Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) was there, and he was one of the happiest men I ever saw. He seemed to be presiding over the completion of the work that was entirely to his liking. I did not think it possible that one who had inveighed against the Trent Valley canal could preside at the opening of that canal with such pleasure. Why, I recollect that we people in Nova Scotia were almost frightened out of our wits that the Conservative government had done something wrong in carrying on this Trent Valley canal work. We trusted the Conserva-

tive party and believed that, in the main, it was right. Still, we feared that, in connection with this matter, there must be something wrong. And the Liberal party in Nova Scotia nsed to tell us : Look at your corrupt government ; look at this infamous ditch in which the public money of Canada was pretended to be spent; that money was not spent, except to be the means of corrupting and debauching the electorate. That was the opinion that hon. gentlemen opposite cultivated for eighteen years. And, even members of the Conservative party almost half believed it. The hon. member for East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) amused me, some time ago, by telling me that, when the Liberals opposed the Conservatives so earnestly, strongly charging them with corruption, even he almost felt like deserting the government, for it seemed impossible that men could bring themselves to carry on such stern opposition, unless they believed something of the charges they were making. Of course, he said he had lived long enough to know that they did not mean a word of what they said. But, such was the earnestness of their advocacy, that even he wavered in his support of Sir John Macdonald, on several occasions. And, if we in Nova Scotia ever wavered in that support, ft was over the question of this Trent Valley canal. So, you can imagine the feeling with which I went up to view this work. And, you can imagine my feelings when I found it to be such a splendid work for the development of the country. I believe in the development of Canada in every part-not less in Ontario and British Columbia than in my own country. I got hold of the map-I love maps and study them always. And, as I studied the map, it was borne in upon my mind that, whether this canal was to carry through freight or not, did not matter, for it is a splendid internal water-way, and will develop an immense country. I devoted a night or two to the study of the map ; and I assure you, Mr. Chairman, my esteem for the province of Ontario was not heightened. We, in Nova Scotia, are apt to believe that the people of Ontario are the narrowest people you can find. And, as I say, my esteem for them was not heightened by my study of this map. Why, you should have had this canal developed eighty years ago. You have settled along the St. Lawrence and taken the little peninsula of western Ontario, but you have left the rest of the country, up to James Bay, almost as bare as when Cartier came. And, you deserve no credit for what has been done. If confederation had not come, you would have been as backward as you were thirty-seven years ago. But, the other provinces have joined you, and have helped to develop your province. I was amazed, when I looked at the map. to think that any man of integrity could have opposed the development of his province by this splendid water-way. Every Mr. GOURLEY.
man in Ontario should have joined to get that country developed thirty or forty years ago. But the great misfortune of Canada is that we talk, and dispute, and decades go by. and nothing is accomplished.
Well, as I say, I went to Peterborough. And I must say that I admired the courage of the Postmaster General (Sir William Mu-lock). Why, his courage was Alpine in its grandeur. For a man who has spent years in opposing this canal to stand up here, and speak in its defence, shows that he possesses the courage of an African lion. And, when I recall the names of McMullen and Cartwright, associated for years with the most deadly opposition to this canal, I admire also the courage of the Conservative party in insisting upon the completion of this scheme. The Conservative party carried every dollar in support of this canal at the point of the bayonet. No Japanese assault was ever bolder, more masterful, or courageous, than the work of the Conservative party in carrying these votes for the Trent Valley canal, against the deadly opposition of their Liberal opponents. Why. these hon. gentlemen opposite must think that the people of Canada have no memories, if they think, for a moment, that we shall lose sight of one of the saddest, and most disgraceful, chapters in Canadian history, the opposition of Ontario Liberals, for eighteen years, to the development of their own province. We always thought that the narrow Liberals of Ontario were opposed to the development of the maritime provinces. We thought that their betfi noir was Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces. But I find that they are equally opposed to the development of Ontario. Bred in a little mould, they could not bear the expenditure of a dollar for public improvement anywhere, even in the province of Ontario. That being the case, I can understand the feelings of contempt that such men as the hon. member for East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane), and the hon. member for Hal-ton (Mr. Henderson), must have for hon. gentlemen opposite. There is such a thing as carrying bravado too far. A statesman should have some sincerity. The Postmaster General would have commended himself more to me if, when this matter was under discussion, he had appeared in habiliments of sackcloth, and with ashes sprinkled on his head. That would have been his proper garb. Had he come here, and said : I have sinned beyond all forgiveness ; but I acknowledge my sin, and, in acknowledging it, I hope I have half won the forgiveness that I crave-had he done that, I would have thought him a man. But when he glories in his sin, when he tries to gain credit by it, he does not add dignity to the public life of Canada. Having seen this great water-way, I heartily support this vote, and I hope my party will support it, as a great work for the development of Canada.
6857 '

I viewed with great pleasure that high lift-lock. The effect of that great engineering work is not confined to Peterborough, it solves many transportation difficulties all over Canada, for instance in the province of Quebec, where rivers drop down from a high plateau to another high plateau. This lift-lock will make the water-ways of Canada available to the commerce of the country. Therefore when I looked upon that magnificent feat of engineering and scientific skill, and remembered that it had been conceived to a large extent in its improved form by the genius of Canadian engineers, I was proud of Canada and of its sons. I am delighted to know that this parliament is charged with the development of more territory than any other parliament in the world, or any other government, barring that of Russia. We have half a continent in charge, we are simply standing at the edge of its development, and in the work of that development we shall find that this lift-lock solves many of the problems that will present themselves to our engineers. Therefore I hail with delight the opening of this lift-lock at Peterborough. X said some harsh things about the Postmaster General, but not intending to say unpleasant things, and X hope that when he looks at this great work and begins to*realize its true meaning, he will ask forgiveness from high Heaven for the awful sins he has committed in not seeing this great work in its true proportions twenty-five years ago, and I hope God will forgive him.
Now my hon. friend seemed to treat with much levity the proposition of having two termini for this water-way. I would like to see half a dozen termini for this water-way. I am not pleading for either one or the other. You can locate them anywhere that will serve the purpose of making a through highway, because then you will want elevators and all the equipments of a port, and I regard this as infinitely valuable as a local and internal water-way. But so narrow minded was the Postmaster General, so bred is he in that little Liberal, Grit, Ontario way of his and of his party, that he could not dream of there being two termini to a great work of this kind. It would burst his head, I fancy, and shatter his brain if he once attempted to conceive it. In many ways 1 admire the hon. Postmaster General, I admire his good nature, and I wonder how a man of some humour can ever be sober when he is speaking and indulging in jokes of that character. I support the idea of two termini, one at Port Hope and one at Trenton ; you can make your third terminus wherever you will ; but in every section of this country where there is a little town growing up. it should be connected with this water-way in the same way.
Now allow me to refer to another thing. My hon. friend said :	Let us get expert
testimony about the settlement of the termini of this water-way system. But I
recollect that when they were proposing to spend two hundred millions of money on the Grand Trunk Pacific system, and we proposed that they get expert testimony before doing so, they refused us, they laughed us to scorn, they said : Let us vote the money, get the railway started, and we will get expert testimony afterwards. That was their position. But hon. gentlemen, in a little matter of this kind, must play the cheap politician and hold this dangling in the air for the purpose of fooling the people of Ontario. I am bound to say that the people of Ontario will be infinitely greater fools than I think they are-and I have not the highest opinion of a great many of them, especially of hon. gentlemen opposite. In the lower provinces we always had an idea that there was a little soft spot in the pates of people of Ontario, but we never dreamed they would go so far as to take the hon. gentleman seriously when he proposes to dangle these two termini before their eyes, without meeting just retribution at their hands. If I were a Liberal of Ontario, after hearing the speech of the Postmaster General this afternoon, I would vote against him and his pary at once and for ever. It is too late in the day for public men to be eternally fooling and scheming about a question of this kind. We want integrity, we want ministers of the Crown, representing the people in this country, to settle these questions on the broad lines of statesmanship and patriotism, then they will be worthy of our confidence.
Now I want to congratulate the ex-Minister of Railways, the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), whom I have learned to respect. I was a stranger when I came into this House, and I had to make up my estimates of men as I met them. I have a very high opinion of the member for South Lanark. He has got convictions, and very few men have them. That is what I admire in him. Right or wrong, you know where to find him. It is a great credit to a man to have convictions about something. The misfortune is that so few of our public men have convictions, but the public man who has them must always be a strong man. But I never knew my hon. friend from South Lanark had such a claim upon the eternal gratitude of the people of this country as to be the father of this great system of the Trent canal. I honour him for supporting it twenty years ago, because at that time there was no Liberal public opinion in Canada. Every little fellow was struggling for his own province. There was no such thing as a man voting for a public work in the interest of the whole of Canada, but he had to vote from the standpoint of his township, or his county, or his province at most. Therefore, when the hon. gentleman started out to carry that canal forward-because it had started years before, but somebody had to carry it forward- and when that hon. gentleman undertook to.

carry it forward he was a brave man, because he had to meet, and oppose, and overcome objections of all sorts from the Liberal party in this House. When he undertook to vote money for this canal he found it a herculean task. Now, after having seen his efforts crowned with so great a measure of success, I hope he will be the father of many other great schemes for the internal development of Canada, and the great Conservative party who has supported him, and will continue to support him, will deserve the utmost credit from the people of this country.
Will the minister tell us about the lift-lock ?

I think there was a question by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) in respect to the route at the Georgian bay end. He referred to the alternative to the Severn, or river route, as it is called. That alternative route, around by Barrie to which he refers) was surveyed some years ago by Mr. Rubidge, an engineer connected with the canals of Canada for a great many years and who has recently died. He had a very large experience in connection with the canal.
A very able man.

So I understand. He surveyed that route and reported, as I have been led to understand, condemnatory of it. He favoured what is known as the river route. I simply call my hon. friend's attention to the fact because he may not have heard of it, or he may not have known that the matter was ever under consideration. It appears that it was. My hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has asked me a question with respect to comparisons between the ordinary lock and the hydraulic lift-lock. One set of ordinary locks would consist of five as compared with one hydraulic lock, or double lock as it is called. The capital cost of one set of five ordinary locks would be $275,000. One hydraulic lock, double set, costs $500,000. The cost of maintenance and wages on the five ordinary locks requiring twenty lockmen, two men to each lock with day and night shifts, each man at $400, is $8,000. The wages in connection with the working of the hydraulic lift-lock would be, for a lock master, one during the day and one at night, and four gatemen, $2,500, as against $8,000 for the five ordinary locks. The annual repairs to the five ordinary locks would be $1,000. They would cost about $250 each.
It would cost $1,250 if there were five locks 1

Yes. The annual repairs to one hydraulic lock are estimated at $100. An element to be considered is the time of locking. With the five ordinary Mr. GOURLEY.
locks, sixty-five feet, one and a half minutes per foot, if will take one and a half hours for one vessel going up or down, or if two vessels go through the locks at the same time it will take one of them one and a half hours, while it will take the other vessel three hours to get through. By the hydraulic lock both vessels will pass through at the same time in twelve minutes. If the saving in wages and repairs, $6,650, in favour of the hydraulic lock over one set of five ordinary locks is capitalized at three per cent it will be equal to a sum considerably above $200,000. This, if deducted from the capital cost of the hydraulic, will leave the cost of the hydraulic lock very little more than the cost of one set of five ordinary locks, while the advantage in the saving of time by the use of the hydraulic lock is vastly greater than by the use of one set of five ordinary locks. These are the views of the engineer, Mr. Rogers, who is in charge of that work and who is certainly to be commended for the efficiency displayed by him in the carrying out of the work.
When will the canal be completed to Lake Simcoe ?
In about a year; when the other hydraulic lift is finished.

The hon. minister has not noticed my question as to whether it is the policy of the government to make immediate provision for the completion of the work not in sections and by dribbling out an amount of money each year, but as I suggested this afternoon by the making of provision for the immediate finishing of the work. I do not know whether the hon. minister takes it seriously. I think he does. Certainly the hon. Postmaster General does not take it seriously and I think the committee is entitled to some explanation as to how it happens that after the boast that has been made by the Postmaster General as to the rapid way in which the present government have been carying on the work, as to the generous way in which they have been providing money to carry on this work, we are only asked for an appropriation of $100,000 at the present time. The hon. Postmaster General says that according to the rate at which we were proceeding under the Conservative administration it would have taken a great many years to complete the work.
Sir WILLIAM MULOCK About two hundred.

That is the hon. gentleman's way of stating it but it does not figure out. According to actual computation, according to the rate at which we are asked to vote money for this enterprise now, it will take at least 150 years to complete the work. Estimating that it

will cost $7,000,000 it will take seventy years by dividing up the time. If you take into consideration that works are always deteriorating as they progress and if you take into account the additional sums of money that will therefore require to be expended during that time it will certainly take a century and a half at the present rate of progress before you may expect the completion of the work. The hon. Postmaster General points out that this work is proving very productive and beneficial at the present time ; in fact he says it is exceedingly beneficial, that this is a magnificent work and one of the greatest possible moment to the people located along the line of that portion of the canal which is now open. But, it is sealed at both ends and it is not a tithe of the benefit to the people that it will be if you open up the two ends. We have been working in the centre and it is the duty of the government to set to work vigorously and open up the ends. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals says that he does not know whether I ever heard of the surveys. Why, I live right alongside of where the surveys have taken place. We know a great deal about the canal, we are interested in it, and I am amazed to think that the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) who is attached to the government has never brought to the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals the fact that the people of North Simcoe are intensely interested in this matter. We have been studying up the reports of the engineers. The people of North Simcoe are greatly interested in the question as to what the Transportation Commission is going to do, and whether the route is by way of Barrie or by the way of Orillia and through Midland by the Severn river, the project is still one of great importance to the people of North Simcoe.
I am amazed that the minister does not realize that all the Simcoes, and especially North Simcoe are interested in this matter. The town of Barrie has the happy fortune of being now associated with South Simcoe, and by reason of my political connection with it in the future, I am urging upon the minister the importance of getting to woific seriously. If this $100,000 for such a work came from any source but the government, I would say it was an insult to the intelligence of the people. Why, when this lift-lock has been opened and connection made between the two stretches of the canal, should this vote be cut down to $100,000 ? The Postmaster General only considers that the public are watching for the expenditure of money in each locality, but I look upon this as a great national work. The people of the United States are watching us and their most eminent engineers are pointing out that this immense improvement should be developed in the interest of Canada, and they are pointing out, too, that it will probably be their greatest competitor for the trade of the western states. At the present time there is every danger, on account of the building of the so-called National Transcontinental Railway, that our trade be diverted to United States ports, and it is more than ever important that we should see to it that our water-ways should serve the purpose for which nature designed them, and that this scheme inaugurated almost a century ago, should not be allowed to lag. Now that there is congestion of traffic in the west it behoves the governments to open up I every avenue of transportation, and the most natural of these avenues is by Lake Superior through the Georgian bay to Montreal and through this very canal. It will not only open up a channel for the commerce of the west, but it will have the effect of compelling railways to largely reduce rates by reason of the competition it affords. I understand that this item is not to pass, as the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Ward) wishes to speak in reference to it, and on my own behalf, until I get certain papers, I would ask the minister to allow it to stand for the present.
I have arranged with the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Ward) to have a discussion on this question, and if the item passes the same opportunity will be given to my hon. friend.
The hon. member for Durham might take the matter up when I am accidently out of the House.
I shall try to arrange that you will be present.
Any way there are several items for the Trent canal.
Can the minister give us an idea as to whether this work will be progressed with rapidly ?

I think I can say that the object is to make progress.
Soulanges canal-survey for breakwater,
This seems a very large sum for a survey. You have the staff on the Galops canal who have done nothing for over a year and surely you can utilize them.

I am advised by the deputy minister that this amount would be necessary. If we take the men from one canal to the other we shall have to charge their services to this work.
Soulanges canal-steel bridge at power house, $4,000.

I want to know the total expenditure on the Soulanges canal and what it costs to work each year. The Auditor General was comparing the cost of the Soulanges canal and the Cornwall canal, and there was a dispute between him and the

Minister of Justice as to a very large amount.

I will give my hon. friend a full statement at next meeting.
Soulanges canal-workshops, heating, lighting and machinery, $7,200.

This includes $4,000 for the steel bridge at the power house over the tail-race. That is the first item. The next is the workshop. $7,000 is for the installation of machinery, wiring, electric lamps, &c. There are about 140 incandescent lamps at forty cents each.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You can buy electric lamps cheaper than that retail.
These are by public tender, advertised in the newspapers. The total estimated cost is $7,200/
Is there anything for the workshops themselves ?
This is simply for lighting and heating and the machinery of the two workshops on the Soulanges canal.
We have it stated in connection with the Cornwall canal that the workshops there will require a large amount of horse-power.
There are two at Cornwall which will require sixty horsepower. This also requires sixty horse-power.
We were told that the workshops to be built at Cornwall were to serve the two canals.
Oh, no. The workshops at Cornwall are to serve the St. Lawrence canals. They are separate altogether,

What is the meaning of this last item of No. 103 7
Appropriation not required for 1904-5, $413,919.37.
I notice that recurring frequently and I would like to know what it means. ,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It means that the columns for the two years would not balance otherwise. That is simply striking a balance from the appropriation of last year. The different items coming under that head which it is not necessary to repeat are lumped together and put in in that way. It is a mere striking of the balance, an aid to comparison, and has no bearing on the estimates of the two years.
It does not balance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is intended to permit of a comparison of the appropriation for the two years.
The column comes to $2,000,000 odd but the corresponding column for 1904-5 is $1,500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In order to show the amount appropriated last year, they take the amount for similar services this year and then in the ease of other services for which no vote is required, they fill in the difference as an explanation of how the total of last year was made up. This practice has been adopted in the preparation of the estimates for generations.
It means that items of a similar class last year are not required this year and the items are added together and inserted in this way ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite correct.
Are the whole final estimates made up and paid on the Soulanges canal now ?

These are the total
estimates.
Are the final estimates made out and settled with the contractors ?
In so far as they can be settled between the department and the contractors they have been, but the contractors have an idea that there are certain additional sums which are due to them.
What I want to know is this. Has the department made its final estimates on the Soulanges canal ?
All except the workshops.
How many men are employed in the workshops ?
We require two or three carpenters and a blacksmith and a machinist.
Have you workshops on the Beauharnois canal ? Where was the work for that canal done before ?
A good deal was done 'at Lachine.
And the workshops on the Cornwall canal did the work for the upper canals ? [DOT]

Yes, on the St. Lawrence canals.
St. Ours lock, constructing new gates,
Where is the work done -at Lachine or on the canal itself ?

This is below St. John's on the Richelieu river. New gates were provided for this lock last year and they were placed in position at the opening of navigation this spring. The old gates are in a dilapidated condition, not fit for service, and this amount is intended to provide spai'e gates. Usually on the canals we keep sets of spare gates in case of accidents. This is to provide the timber and $6,000 is the

estimate. The timber is estimated to cost $2,410 ; the castings are estimated to cost $700, the steel $140, the paints and oils $250, and labour $2,500.
Let by contract ?

No, done by the men employed on the canal. We must have men there to make these constant repairs. A great deal of the material in the old gates is good, especially the timber, and we put in new timber just as you would put in new ribs in a wooden vessel. You could not have this work done by contract.
This is not a question of repairs, but of constructing new gates.

These new gates are made by the men in the employ. It was necessary to keep them to make repairs to the old gates, and as they are there it is cheaper to utilize them in making the new gates than to give out the contract.
I venture to say that the hon. gentleman will find that it would be much less expensive to have this work done by contract. This is a most improvident way of doing the work.
How much money was expended there last year ?
There was nothing expended last year on that item, because there was no appropriation.
Are these new gates made at the shops in Lachine or on the St. Lawrence canal ?

In the workshops at Ghambly. A good deal of the work is done in the winter, and these men employed in the summer are given employment in the winter in connection with this work.
Carillon and Grenville canal-rebuilding -Grenville wharf (revote), $23,000.

This wharf was built twenty-one years ago. The part above water is in urgent need of being renewed. It is proposed to replace the cribwork with concrete. The whole amount was voted last year, but became available too late to be used during the year.
Will this $23,000 finish the work ?
That is the estimate. It is intended to invite tenders.
What did the wharf cost before ?
It was built twenty-one years ago, and I have not the figures as to the cost.

The portion under water ought to be as good as ever, and all that would need repairing would be the upper
part. This seems an enormous sum for such work.
The cribwork is to be replaced with concrete, which makes it much more expensive.
But it is only the part above water that is to be replaced, not the whole cribwork.
It is a good portion of it.
And this is a good price. It must be a large wharf when the part above water costs $23,000.
This is the estimate of the engineer. But the work is to be put up for tender, and I suppose there will-be competition. Of course, the lowest tender will be accepted.
I understood the hon. minister to say that no money was spent at St. Ours Locks last year. But I would draw his attention to the fact that $800 was voted last year. Was not that expended ?
Not in connection with the gates at St. Ours.

I did not say for the gates. I asked if there was any money expended.
MB. EMMERSON.	There were two
wharfs repaired in that lock last year.
What was the total cost ?
I have not that information.
Would the expenditure be at the same point ?
Yes, at the same point-the St. Ours canal.
I understood the minister to say there was expenditure for new gates last year. What was the necessity for that ?

That was in the appropriation of the year previous. There was no appropriation in 1903-4. Of course, I was reading the explanation given by the engineer, and this explanation, of course was prepared last fall.
Under what item can we find the explanation of the $800 ?
I will bring a statement of the expenditure for my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) if he wishes it.

Oh, no.
Welland canal-stone protection to banks of new canal, $20,000.

It is represented that the rip-rap protection of the banks of the new canal has not been renewed since it was first placed about twenty years ago ? It is all worn away in many places and the banks have been cut by the action of the

water. It is estimated that $20,000 will renew the rip-rap protection on ten miles of the bank.
Will this work be let by tender ?

Yes.
Welland canal-to change valves and hanging gear of new Welland canal lock gates, $30,000.

This is to change the Townsend valve, which never worked satisfactorily, being complicated, easily put out of repair and slow. This valve is being replaced with what is known as the butterfly valve. The valves are placed at the bottom of the gates. There are twenty-seven locks, in over half of which the valves have been replaced. The amount expended up to last May, 1904, was $14,498.62. The work is being done by the canal staff. The full expenditure on the work does not appear in the amount I have named. The account was not kept separately, the expenditure charged up to the vote to execute heavy repairs.
How long has the Townsend valve been used ?

This work is at Ramey's Bend. The expenditure becomes necessary because the deepening along the side of the present wall which is now going on tends to bring the wall down. It is .already falling in places. It is proposed to build a concrete wall founded on the new bottom of the canal at a cost of $70,000.
Has the contract been let ?

Yes.
Lachine canal-rebuilding old Locks 1 and 2, $45,000.

This is to rebuild and lengthen or extend the walls of the old locks 1 and 2 at Montreal. The walls were falling into decay, and becoming unsafe. This is contract work, Quinlan & Robertson are the contractors. This amount will complete the work. It is expected the locks will be ready for navigation in the course of the present season. The total expenditure up to the 1st of May last was $143,014. The estimated cost is $213,000. The work is certainly very necessary. It is all let by contract. Both locks were old. There are many market boats that go down through them.

I thought there was a plan for utilizing the old locks of the canal, Mr. EMMERSON.
taking them down altogether and building virtually a docking place for ships.

There is a basin formed there which is to be utilized for the purpose my hon. friend mentions.
Lachine canal-under-pinning wall, basin No. 2, $7,000.

This work can only be done during the period when the canal is unwatered in the spring, a short period of about a month. The foundation of the new wall will probably be completed in a couple of seasons, after which it is expected the balance of the work will occupy two summers.
Lachine canal-lock gates, $10,000.

This is required for repairs and for spare gates for the new locks. It is usual to keep on hand spare gates in case of accident.
Soulanges canal-arms for gates and heaters, $1,350.
We require five spare arms for operating the gates, costing $50 each. Then we want 12 electric heaters, costing $30 each, 13 transformers, costing $50 each ; and the wiring is estimated to cost $140.

I would like'you to bring down the amount expended on the power-house and the amount expended for electrical purposes, both for power and for lighting that canal. I want these amounts for the purpose of comparison with the expenditure on the Cornwall canal.
Soulanges canal-water-wheel governors and heaters, $1 500. 1

We want to put in two new culverts at $400 each ; remove the old culverts and settle the new ones, $100 ; 6 electric heaters, at $40 each ; 6 transformers, at $50 each ; wiring, $60.
Soulanges canal-widening and deepening St. Amour's gully, $4,000.

This gully is about two miles above the lower entrance to the canal. The soil is very soft. There is a ditch which was not made deep and wide enough at first, and is now choked ; and in order to avoid damages to the adjoining farms by back water, this work is necessary. It is to be done. During the present season we expect to do the excavation, stone-lining, sodding and alterations to culverts.

Are they under the canal ?
iMr. EMMERSON. The culverts are under the canal. It is to prevent water doing damage to the farms.
We have had an enormous expenditure on the Soulanges for the purpose of taking that river under the canal.
That is not the place. I
But I do not know of any other place in which drains passed along the canal.
This is on section 3 of O'Leary's contract.
Was there a drain before the canal was constructed ?
Yes, there was a natural water-course, but they carried more water into it by reason of the ditches on the side of the canal.
This work is all done by tender ?
Yes.
Wherever you construct a canal you have to drain the whole neighbourhood ?

Yes, and then you have claims for damages for injuring property.
Chambly canal-to extend and repair wall at head of Ste. Therese island, $2,200.

This work is necessary and the money is required to provide a boulder line on the slope above the piece of wall built in the last three years to protect the head of the island against the action of the Richelieu river. The water in the river, a year ago last spring, rose to an unprecedented height and the necessity of protecting the slope above the wall became apparent. There was $900 provided last year. Up to May 1st, it is estimated there has been $748.29 expended. We will require $2,200 more this year.
The hon. minister seems to have branched out a good deal since last year. Last year $900 was all that was required.

Yes, but that was for a separate wall. That wall was completed but this is for an additional wall to line the slope above the wall already built with small boulders extending about 1,400 feet, the total estimated cost of which is $2,200.
This is something that has developed since last year ?
Yes.
And this $2,200 will complete the work ?
That is the estimated cost.
It will be let by contract ?

It will be let by tender.
Chambly canal-to rebuild culvert, Renault's farm, $8,000.
That is a large sum for a farm. You had better buy the farm and make a present of it to some one.

The culvert has been giving a good deal of trouble owing to leaks. It was examined during last winter and the timbers were found to be in a decayed and rotten condition, so much so that it is necessary to rebuild it. It is proposed to rebuild it of concrete as was done in the case of other culverts on this canal in the last few years. The excavation is ex-timated at $1,800. Other items are the removal of the old culvert, concrete and unwatering, the whole being estimated at $8,000. This is not for the protection of one farm.
What is the object of the culvert ? Does it drain more than one farm ?
This culvert is under the canal and there is very much more than one farm drained but it is located on De-nault's farm, it is given that name.
Will that work be let by tender ?
Yes.
Has there been any money spent on that work in the last three or four years ?

No.
Chambly canal-to macadamize road west side of canal, $4,000.
There was an appropriation last year. It is estimated that the materials and labour for the one and a quarter miles necessary to be done will cost $4,000.
What are you macadamizing it for ?

They say the road is almost impassable during wet weather. During the construction of the canal the earth was removed from the side and used in the building of that tow path. It has spoiled the road. At some seasons of the year the water in the canal comes up to within a foot or two of the road and makes the road soft and wet. The highway is on government property. About a mile of the road was macadamized in 1873. The macadamized tow path extends on the east side of the canal between St. .Tohn's, lock No. 1 and Chambly lock No. 2.
This is on the west side?
Yes.
Is this a tow-path simply?
Oh. no. This is a road built for the benefit of the people of the country.
This runs parallel to the canal 1
Yes.
Is the government expected to build these roads alongside of the canal for the accommodation of the public ?
In building the canal they injured the road.
And this is making good the injury ?

This makes good the injury. The road is impassable practically by reason of the act of the government in Duilding the canal. Now it is necessary to macadamize the road in order that the public may get the benefit of it.
Will the 'government have to maintain this road for all time ?
Part of this was done as far back as 1873.
I say will the government have to maintain this road for all time ?
Yes.

If you encroach upon the road in building the canal you should restore it'to its original condition, but I think the maintenance of the road should fall upon the municipality. What appears to be done in this ease is that the government is keeping up at the expense of the country this highway which I think should be maintained at the expense of the municipality.

The water in the canal has been raised since the canal was built. The lock-gates were raised and the height of the water was raised with the result that the soakage into the bank does great injury to the road.
The country seems to be getting soaked in this case.
They think that the government rather than the road should be soaked. Perhaps there is some equity in it.
I dare say.

If it is by reason of the water rising it is quite proper to restore the road to a proper condition, but I do not think tlje government ought to keep it in repair unless some new condition arises. The ordinary repair of the road should fall upon the municipality.

If I remember rightly when I was minister there was a petition to have this road repaired. I think I got a report from the officer down there as to the liability of the government and I found that they had none. In fact I went over part of it myself when I was down there Mr. HAGGART.
and I did not see any liability on the part of the government. The damages were paid for and the repairs made after the canal was built. It is alleged now, as the bon. minister says and it was alleged in my time, that the height of the water some how or other had increased in the canal. I do not think that is so. The man in charge of the waste weir has reported that there lias been no increased water in it since the canal was built.

I am informed by the deputy minister that there is no doubt the water was raised by the raising of the lock. The damage done to the individuals was paid for, but there is constant soakage from the canal to the road, and it is necessary to macadamize it.
Has the work been done ?
About a mile was done last year, and there is about a mile and a quarter to do.
It costs 83,000 a mile ?

Yes.
Sir. (LENNOX. The people of the country will be amazed when they find it takes 83,000 a mile to macadamize a road.
It is done by contract and tender.
Perhaps you are asphalting it.
No ; macadamizing.
It is time to give the government warning that the people will not be satisfied to pay $3,000 a mile for macadamizing a road.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Vote the money ; it is the last chance the government will have.
There is something in that, but if the minister does get a chance I hope he will not do it again.

The cost of the macadam would depend upon how the work was done. If it is an ordinary country road $3,000 a mile would be an outrageous amount, but if it is made with broken rock it would be different. What is the character of the work ?	-	- -
It is macadamized with broken stone.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What depth of broken stone ?

I have not the specifications here.
Chambly canal-renewing landing wharf,

Ml-. ESISIERSON. The old wharf is beyond repair. The action of the ice each spring is very damaging, but with concrete walls and steel girders the work will be of

a permanent character, except the timber flooring.
Will this complete ?
Yes.
We appear to have voted $6,000 for this last year.
No ; there are two wharfs, one above and one below the locks, and this is for the one above the locks.
Is it time we were adjourning ?
I thought, if these items were not controversial, we would probably get through with them.
We cannot. Have you brought down the information we asked for the other day in reference to the Galops canal ?
Yes, I think so. Here is the Gilbert contract ?
Of what year ?

1897. This is the only contract. I asked the deputy for all the contracts with regard to these matters and he gave me these papers as copies of all there were.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What do you intend doing on Monday ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We propose going into supply and taking up the estimates of the Interior Department.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 10.45 p.m.
Monday, July 18, 1904.
